claims.claim: The FDA approved DES on 19 September 1941 for four indications including menopausal symptoms.
claims.episode_span: The FDA had approved DES for menopausal symptoms in 1941 and, on 1 July 1947, explicitly approved its use in pregnancy
claims.supporting_quote: It was approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on September 19, 1941, in tablets up to 5 mg for four indications: gonorrheal vaginitis , atrophic vaginitis , menopausal symptoms, and postpartum lactation suppression to prevent breast engorgement.

claims.claim: On 1 July 1947 the FDA approved DES for use in pregnancy to prevent adverse pregnancy outcomes.
claims.episode_span: on 1 July 1947, explicitly approved its use in pregnancy — this was sanctioned practice, not off-label improvisation
claims.supporting_quote: On July 1, 1947, the FDA approved the use of DES for this indication. The first such approval was granted to Bristol-Myers Squibb

claims.claim: The study linking prenatal DES exposure to clear-cell adenocarcinoma of the vagina in daughters was published in the New England Journal of Medicine on 22 April 1971, led by Arthur Herbst.
claims.episode_span: In 1971, Arthur Herbst, Howard Ulfelder and David Poskanzer published a case-control study in the New England Journal of Medicine
claims.supporting_quote: The research study that changed everything was published on April 22, 1971 in the New England Journal of Medicine . Arthur Herbst et al, linked prenatal DES exposure to a rare vaginal cancer in girls and young women – clear cell adenocarcinoma (CCA).

claims.claim: The 1971 report's authors were Herbst, Ulfelder and Poskanzer ('Adenocarcinoma of the vagina').
claims.episode_span: In 1971, Arthur Herbst, Howard Ulfelder and David Poskanzer published a case-control study in the New England Journal of Medicine
claims.source_title: DES Case Study - Women and Health Research - NCBI Bookshelf
claims.supporting_quote: Herbst, A.L., Ulfelder, H., and Poskanzer, D.C. 1971. Adenocarcinoma of the vagina.

claims.claim: In November 1971 the FDA moved against the use of DES during pregnancy in the US (Drug Bulletin to physicians; pregnancy made a contraindication).
claims.episode_span: On 10 November 1971 the FDA advised physicians that DES was contraindicated in pregnancy.
claims.source_title: Diethylstilbestrol (DES) in the US | Embryo Project Encyclopedia
claims.supporting_quote: in November of 1971, the FDA banned the use of DES during pregnancy in the US

claims.claim: Charles Dodds himself warned against introducing DES into the female reproductive cycle and stressed its possible cancer-causing effects.
claims.episode_span: Charles Dodds, the British biochemist who first synthesized DES, himself warned against its use in pregnancy
claims.source_title: Diethylstilbestrol (DES) in the US | Embryo Project Encyclopedia
claims.supporting_quote: However, Dodds said that the human female reproductive cycle was too delicate to introduce foreign substances into it, and he denounced the use of DES to prevent or end pregnancies. Dodds stressed the possible cancerous effects of DES and other synthetic estrogens.

claims.claim: A 1957 medical-journal advertisement for the DES brand desPLEX promised 'bigger and stronger babies, too.'
claims.episode_span: Professional journals carried advertisements promising “bigger and stronger babies.”
claims.source_title: Healthy Baby Ad | DES Action USA
claims.supporting_quote: 96 percent live delivery with desPLEX in one series of 1200 patients – bigger and stronger babies, too.

claims.claim: An estimated 5 to 10 million women were exposed to DES (the NIH figure is scoped to the United States; the digest states it as a worldwide figure).
claims.episode_span: by the mid-1950s an estimated five to ten million women worldwide had received the drug during gestation
claims.source_title: Diethylstilbestrol and its Multigenerational Effects - AWIS
claims.supporting_quote: According to the NIH, 5 to 10 million women in the United States had exposure to DES.
